doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Kenton's reputation, Dizzy's criticism and Monk's defense
summary: Konitz thinks Kenton was treated unfairly; Kirchner tells the Monk story at Berlin, and they mention Kenton's popular hits.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Yeah. Nobody plays his music on the radio that I hear. When I heard recently that Wynton was going to play next February, they’ve invited Bill Holman to come and asked me to play a couple tunes. They did some nice music especially Bill Holman’s music, Gerry Mulligan’s music, Bill Russo did some interesting things. I thought that was unjust. There seemed to be some . . . Dizzy seemed to be putting Stan on for some black and white reason I think.
Can I tell you a lovely story?

At the Berlin Jazz Festival around nineteen sixty nine or seventy, Thelonious Monk was there and Kenton’s band was also on the bill, and Monk overheard somebody, who’ll remain nameless, putting down Kenton; a white guy as it happened. Monk turned to the guy and said: “what’ve you done compared to what he’s done?”
There’s Kenton music you can like or dislike.
Of course “Peanut Vendor”. We had to live with that as apart of his money making piece.
“Tampico”. Those were his bread and butter songs.
But he hired a lot of good players and gave a lot of good writers their break like Holman or Lenny Niehaus, or Rugolo, or Graettinger, on and on. Let’s talk about the experience you had.
